record.paper_title: Autonomous Agents Modelling Other Agents: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can an autonomous agent learn to identify, track, and predict another agent's behaviour when that behaviour may change during the interaction—for example because the other agent is adapting, learning, switching strategies, or is human—rather than remaining fixed or stationary throughout the encounter?

evidence.quote: Hence, the design of methods which can effectively learn to identify, track, and predict changing behaviours remains a significant open problem, one which will be a crucial element in the quest for full autonomy.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an autonomous agent A interacting over discrete time steps t = 1, 2, ... with another agent B in a shared environment modeled as a (partially observable) stochastic game. At each time t, agent A observes some signal o_t (which may include B's actions, joint outcomes, and environmental state) and must maintain a model M_t of agent B that allows A to (i) identify B's current behavioural type or policy, (ii) track changes to that policy over time, and (iii) predict B's next action a_t^B given history.

Unlike the standard assumption that B follows a fixed (stationary) policy π : S → Δ(A_B), suppose instead that B's policy is non-stationary: B may be adapting, learning, deliberately switching among a (possibly unknown) set of strategies, or may be a human whose behaviour drifts over time. Formally, B's behaviour is a sequence of policies (π_t)_{t≥1} that may change as a function of the interaction history, with no a priori bound on the number, frequency, or magnitude of such changes, and with the underlying class of policies not assumed to be known to A.

Design a learning and modelling framework for agent A that, in this setting, provably (or empirically, with quantifiable guarantees) achieves the three objectives above. Concretely, give an algorithm that produces predictions p_t(a | history) of B's next action together with performance guarantees—e.g., bounds on online predictive regret or KL-loss relative to the true non-stationary policy sequence (π_t), detection guarantees for changes in π_t, and consistency guarantees for any inferred latent type or strategy index—under the weakest possible structural assumptions on how π_t may evolve. Equivalently: characterize the structural conditions on the variation of (π_t) that are necessary and sufficient for such guarantees to be achievable.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as a significant open problem in agent modelling: designing methods that effectively identify, track, and predict another agent's changing (non-stationary) behaviour. While related subproblems (non-stationary bandits, opponent modelling in games, change-point detection, meta-learning against adaptive opponents) have substantial partial results, no general framework with provable guarantees under arbitrary behavioural change exists, and recent surveys continue to list this as an unresolved challenge.
